The delay is also asymmetric within each revolution: as a side's gain falls toward zero, its delay lengthens toward the maximum, and as the sound comes back round it shortens again, which is how one continuous signal manages to sound as though it passes in front of the listener and then behind. Because all of that happens across the two channels rather than within either one, the downmix to mono at the start costs nothing, and the output has to be stereo for the effect to exist at all. Headphones are the right way to listen to it and speakers are the wrong way: with two speakers in a room, both ears hear both speakers, the interaural delay is filled in by the room and by the head's own shadow, and the effect collapses into a plain pan. Slower rotations also sound more natural, since a fast spin is heard as an effect rather than as movement.

What it does not do:

- No head-related transfer function, so no height information is created.
- No front or rear distance cues beyond the rotation itself.
- Genuine stereo sources are reduced to mono before processing.
- No automatic rotation based on the material's tempo or structure.
- The effect disappears on speakers.
- Output is sixteen bit WAV.

Use it for the sound it is named after, which listeners recognise from music uploads: a track that sweeps past the ears once per revolution, or a spoken passage that circles the listener for a moment of interest. When the movement should be a one-off pass rather than a continuing orbit, the doppler effect simulator sends the source past at a chosen speed, and when the space should be wider without any movement at all, the stereo widener works on the image in place.
howTo: Drop an audio file onto the panel and let it decode.
Choose the rotation time, using a longer one for a subtler sweep.
Set the depth, which controls the ear delay and therefore how convincing the circle is.
Convert the file and listen on headphones, since the effect is invisible on speakers.
whenToUse: 8D Audio Converter is the tool for the rotating, headphone-only movement that gives the effect its name. {{doppler-effect-simulator|Doppler Effect Simulator}} sends a sound past the listener once at a chosen speed rather than around them. When width rather than movement is what a mix needs, {{stereo-widener|Stereo Widener}} changes the image in place, and {{surround-sound-simulator|Surround Sound Simulator}} builds discrete rear channels for a four-speaker system.

faqs.q: Why does it need headphones?
faqs.a: Because the whole effect is the difference between what each ear receives. With two speakers, each ear hears both of them, the small interaural delay is filled in by the room and by the listener's own head, and the movement collapses into an ordinary pan that any stereo mix has.

faqs.q: What does the depth control change?
faqs.a: The maximum delay applied between the ears, which is about two thirds of a millisecond at full depth. That interval is close to the natural arrival-time difference for a sound at one side of the head, so reducing it weakens the sense of direction until the effect becomes a simple panning sweep.

faqs.q: Does a stereo source survive the conversion?
faqs.a: Its stereo image does not, since the source is averaged to mono before being spun. That is inherent to the effect: the rotation supplies the spatial information, and leaving the original image in place would compete with it rather than add to it.

faqs.q: Why is a slower rotation more natural?
faqs.a: Because a sound circling the head several times a second is heard as an effect rather than as movement, and its direction becomes a blur. A revolution taking eight seconds or more reads as a source travelling around a room, which is what the effect is imitating.

faqs.q: Does it create height or front-to-back depth?
faqs.a: No, it works on one horizontal circle. There is no head-related transfer function, so no elevation is produced and distance is conveyed only by the movement itself rather than by any change in tone or directness.

intro: Slowed + Reverb, Nightcore produces the two classic edits in one place: a slowed copy that drops in pitch with a reverb behind it, or a nightcore lift that takes the tempo and pitch up together.
content:
Choose a style, set the speed, and create the edit. Both are remixes in the tape tradition, a slowdown and a speed up, each of which takes the pitch of the music with it; in the slowed style a reverb is added to the result, and in the nightcore style the sped-up copy is left dry.

The styles and the controls:

- Slowed, with a speed from sixty to a hundred percent of the original, defaulting to eighty five, and a reverb mix from nothing to sixty percent, defaulting to thirty five.
- Nightcore, with a speed from a hundred and five to a hundred and fifty percent, and no reverb.
- A report giving the speed as a percentage, the equivalent pitch movement in cents, either the reverb mix and its tail length or simply that the result is dry, and the output duration.

Both styles are built on one piece of arithmetic that is worth understanding, because it is the reason these edits sound the way they do. The speed change is a resample, the same operation a tape machine performs when it runs at the wrong speed: playing the sample data faster or slower makes the music move faster or slower and moves its pitch in exactly the same proportion. That is why a slowed copy sounds lower as well as slower and a nightcore copy sounds higher as well as faster, and it is the opposite of the time stretching that a tempo changer does, where pitch and duration are separated. The report states the pitch side directly in cents, which for the default slowed setting of eighty five percent works out at about two hundred and eighty cents down. Two hundred and eighty cents is a little under three semitones, which is why a slowed track so often ends up in a different key from the original. The slowed style then adds a reverb with a fixed character: a small room of a little over a second, a long feedback and damping that removes the top end of the tail, mixed at the level you set, with a two-second tail that rings past the end of the music. That tail is the reason the style is named for the reverb as much as for the speed, since it is what turns a slowed loop into something that sounds like a live recording. The nightcore style skips the reverb because the effect it imitates does too: the point there is brightness and energy rather than space.

Where it is limited:

- The speed change moves the pitch with it, so the key changes as well as the tempo.
- One reverb character, with only its level adjustable.
- Two fixed speed ranges, one below and one above the original.
- The reverb tail extends the file beyond the music rather than being trimmed to its length.
- No separate control of pitch and duration.
- Output is sixteen bit WAV.

Use it when the edit itself is the goal: the slowed, reverb-backed version that has become a genre of its own, or the brighter faster lift of nightcore. When the tempo should change without the pitch moving, the tempo changer separates the two, and when only the pitch should move, the pitch shifter and the pitch shift calculator are the tools for that. When a different reverb character is wanted, the convolution reverb and the reverb simulator offer more control than the fixed tail here.
howTo: Drop an audio file onto the panel and let it decode.
Choose the slowed style or the nightcore one, which determines the available speed range.
Set the speed, and in the slowed style the reverb mix as well.
Create the edit, then check the reported cents figure if the key change matters.
whenToUse: Slowed + Reverb, Nightcore is the tool for the two named edits, pitch and tempo moving together as they do on tape. {{tempo-changer|Tempo Changer}} changes the speed without moving the pitch, and {{audio-pitch-shifter|Audio Pitch Shifter}} moves the pitch without changing the duration. When the reverb should be chosen rather than fixed, {{convolution-reverb|Convolution Reverb}} and {{reverb-simulator|Reverb Simulator}} give the controls this edit deliberately does not.

faqs.q: Why does the pitch change with the speed?
faqs.a: Because the edit is a resample, the same thing that happens when a tape machine runs at the wrong speed. Playing the samples faster makes the music faster and raises its pitch by the same proportion, which is what gives both these edits their character.

faqs.q: How far does the pitch move?
faqs.a: The report states it in cents, and the arithmetic is straightforward: the default slowed setting of eighty five percent works out at about two hundred and eighty cents down, which is a little under three semitones and often puts the track in a different key from the original.

faqs.q: Why does nightcore not use the reverb?
faqs.a: Because the effect it imitates is dry. A nightcore edit is about brightness, tempo and a higher pitch, and adding a wet tail would work against that by blurring the transients that the speed increase has sharpened.

faqs.q: Why does the output run past the music?
faqs.a: Because the reverb tail keeps ringing after the source has finished, and cutting it off at the music's end would produce an abrupt stop. Some listeners trim the tail afterwards, which is fine; leaving it in is the more natural result.

faqs.q: Can I slow the track without changing its key?
faqs.a: Not here, since the edit is defined by the pitch moving with the tempo. Slowing at the same pitch requires time stretching instead, which is what the tempo changer does, and the result will sound smoother but will lose the tape character that makes these styles recognisable.
